newsitem.title: UK: FIMAT committed to LME ring, will develop business.
newsitem.headline: FIMAT committed to LME ring, will develop business.

text.p: Fimat Metals Ltd, effectively the newest ring-dealing member of the London Metal Exchange (LME), is fully committed to floor trading and will further develop its business, company executives said in an interview.
Fimat Metals is wholly-owned by Fimat International Banque, which is a 100-percent subsidiary of France's Societe Generale Group.
The unit was formed in late September 1996 - as a result of Fimat buying U.S. commodity trader Brody White.

"Since then (September 1996) the company has been completely revamped. It is important to focus on our needs within the group. So far, the results have been good, and the integration has worked well," Olivier Godin, Fimat Metals Managing Director said.
Meanwhile, Fimat's business has increased markedly at a time when turnovers in some LME contracts, such as copper, have fallen, Fimat senior trader Bill Miller said.
"One of the reasons for our success is the confidential approach to the way we do business and buld up trust with our customers," he said.
"Fimat went from being one of the smallest LME ring-dealers as Brody White to one of the largest," Mark Slade, director of Fimat's LME division said.

The company has expanded its staff at a time when virtually no other firms are increasing their mumbers. Fimat has also opened a New York office - at a time when the overall metals market is suffering from the post-Sumitomo hangover.
Last June, Japan's Sumitomo Corp rocked the metals world by announcing losses eventually put at $2.6 billion due to alleged unauthorised trading by its former head trader Yasuo Hamanaka.
The LME has been hit by falling turnovers, with two companies - Lehman Brothers Commodities last November and Deutsche Sharps Pixley last week - relinquishing their ring-membership.
"The Sumitomo affect is still being felt in the market, and you will see unusual trading conditions for at least another year. But the market will take this pain and will be stronger," Slade said.
"We think that the LME is a strong market, although there should be more done to attract people to the ring," he added.
Another impact of the Sumitomo affair is that companies are taking a much harder look at the risks involved in proprietary trading in relation to their net worth, Godin said.
"There will be more care taken by firms against risk exposure with counter-parties. I think that this is benficial, but it is an expensive process," he added.
